description: Design-This-Yourself interactive challenges with hidden entity checklists, diagrams, and reference C++ solutions.

topics.title: Practice 1: Tic-Tac-Toe Game Engine
topics.definition: An interactive $N \times N$ multiplayer Tic-Tac-Toe game engine supporting customizable board sizes, arbitrary winning streak rules ($K$ in a row), Undo/Redo moves via Command Pattern, and AI bot players.
topics.why_it_matters: Frequent warm-up LLD question at Microsoft and Amazon. Tests grid representations, win-checking algorithms in $O(1)$ time, and extensible player strategies.
topics.real_world_analogy: Classic paper-and-pencil game generalized to an $N$-dimensional tournament board with move replay logs.
conceptual_breakdown: Board Entity: $N \times N$ grid with row, column, and diagonal counter arrays for $O(1)$ win checking.

classes.name: Board
methods: + makeMove(r: int, c: int, piece: char): bool
+ checkWin(r: int, c: int, piece: char): bool

steps.description: Player X places piece at (0, 0). rowCounts[0]++, diag++.
Player O places piece at (1, 1). rowCounts[1]--, diag--.
Player X places at (0, 1) and (0, 2). rowCounts[0] reaches +3 == N.
Game transitions to WON. Player X wins in O(1) check time!

step_by_step_explanation: 1. O(1) Win Checking Algorithm: By maintaining row, column, and diagonal counters ($+1$ for X, $-1$ for O), checking if a move won takes $O(1)$ time rather than $O(N)$ row/column scans.
2. Player Rotation Queue: A std::deque handles multiplayer turns cleanly via pop_front() and push_back().
3. Clean Encapsulation: The Board manages grid boundaries and move validation, while TicTacToeGame orchestrates turns.

common_mistakes.mistake: Running full O(N^2) board scans after every turn

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How would you support an N*N board where winning requires only K in a row (e.g. 5-in-a-row on 19x19 Go board)?'
Answer: Accumulator counters only work for $K=N$. For $K < N$, use directional ray casting sliding window checking $K$ steps in 4 axes from the placed coordinate.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor hardcoded 2-player turn logic into an arbitrary N-player queue.

practice_problem.title: Add Move Undo/Redo via Command Pattern
practice_problem.description: Implement `undo()` and `redo()` on `TicTacToeGame` using a `std::vector<MoveCommand>` stack.
practice_problem.hint: Each MoveCommand stores `(r, c, piece)`. Undo resets grid spot and decrements accumulators.

topics.title: Practice 2: Snake & Ladder Multiplayer Game
topics.definition: A complete multiplayer board game simulation featuring variable board sizes, snake and ladder jump mappings, multi-dice rolling strategies, and winner ranking.
topics.why_it_matters: Tests composition, Strategy Pattern for dice rolling, and graph/lookup jump resolution.
topics.real_world_analogy: Classic board game with 100 tiles where landing on tile 14 slides you down to 7 (Snake) or tile 9 shoots you up to 31 (Ladder).
conceptual_breakdown: Board Entity: Array of cells or Jump Map unordered_map mapping start tile to destination tile.
Dice Rolling Strategy: IDiceStrategy (e.g. Standard 1-6 Dice, Loaded Dice, 2-Dice sum).
Game Engine Loop: Roll dice $\to$ advance position $\to$ apply jump $\to$ check win ($position == totalCells$).

steps.description: Player 1 at tile 12 rolls a 4 -> moves to tile 16.
Tile 16 has a Ladder to 35 -> Player climbs to tile 35.
Player 2 at tile 48 rolls a 5 -> moves to tile 53 (Snake to 10). Slides down to 10.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Unified Jump Representation: Storing both snakes and ladders in a single unordered_map simplifies jump logic without requiring distinct classes.
2. Strategy Pattern for Dice: IDiceStrategy makes testing deterministic with mocked dice rolls.
3. Exact Finish Rule: Handles boundary over-rolls ($pos + roll > target$) cleanly.

common_mistakes.mistake: Infinite jump cycles (Snake at 20 -> 10, Ladder at 10 -> 20)
common_mistakes.correction: Validate acyclic DAG graph invariants when inserting jumps.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Can a player land on a snake that drops them into another ladder in the same turn?'
Answer: Clarify whether jump chaining is allowed. If yes, replace `if (jump)` with `while (jump)` guarded by an iteration depth limit.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor hardcoded `rand() % 6 + 1` dice rolls into an injectable IDiceStrategy interface.

practice_problem.title: Design Minimum Dice Rolls BFS Solver
practice_problem.description: Add a method `int findShortestPathToWin()` that uses BFS to find the minimum number of dice rolls needed to win from tile 1.
practice_problem.hint: Model the 100 tiles as an unweighted directed graph and run standard BFS.

topics.title: Practice 3: Multi-recipe Coffee Machine
topics.definition: An interactive smart coffee brewing system managing raw ingredient inventory (water, milk, coffee beans), recipe customization, dynamic price calculation, and parallel brewing dispensers.
topics.why_it_matters: Demonstrates the Decorator Pattern (condiments like Extra Foam, Caramel drizzle), Factory Pattern (Espresso, Latte, Cappuccino), and Inventory Invariant validation.
topics.real_world_analogy: A Starbucks automated barista kiosk that tracks milliliter levels of steamed milk and grams of ground espresso, warning staff when milk is depleted.
conceptual_breakdown: Ingredient & Inventory: Inventory managing thread-safe counts of Water, Milk, Beans, Sugar.
Beverage Decorator Pattern: Beverage base with Espresso, wrapped by MochaDecorator, WhipDecorator.
Recipe Engine: Defines required ingredients per drink.
Brewing Execution: Validates and deducts stock atomically before dispensing.

steps.description: CoffeeMachine deducts 50ml Water, 30g Beans, 50ml Milk and dispenses.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Dynamic Composition via Decorator: Allows combining arbitrary condiments (Mocha, Milk, Caramel) at runtime without creating $2^N$ subclass permutations.
2. Recursive Cost Calculation: Calling getCost() delegates down the decorated chain, summing base beverage and all condiment prices cleanly.
3. Atomic Inventory Deduction: Verification and deduction happen under a single mutex lock to avoid partial ingredient consumption.

comparison_matrix.title: Beverage Modeling Approaches
rows: Violated (must edit base class for new condiments)

common_mistakes.mistake: Deducting water first, failing on beans, and leaving water deducted (Dirty State)
common_mistakes.correction: Verify ALL required ingredients exist before deducting any of them.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How do you handle multiple cups brewing simultaneously on a 3-spout machine?'
Answer: Introduce a thread pool of SpoutWorkers with a semaphore(3) guarding concurrent dispenser spouts.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a beverage class using 15 boolean condiment flags into a clean Decorator hierarchy.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: class Coffee { bool hasMilk, hasMocha, hasCaramel; double getCost() { ... } };

practice_problem.title: Design Low-Inventory Alert System
practice_problem.description: Implement an Observer pattern that sends an alert to the Barista when any ingredient drops below 10% capacity.

topics.title: Practice 4: Asynchronous Logging Framework
topics.definition: A high-throughput non-blocking asynchronous logging framework buffering log events in memory and flushing to multiple sinks (Console, File, Socket) via a dedicated background worker thread.
topics.why_it_matters: One of the most practical systems design questions. Tests Producer-Consumer concurrency, Chain of Responsibility (Log Level filtering), and Observer/Strategy for Log Appenders.
topics.real_world_analogy: Log4j / Spdlog: application worker threads push log strings into an in-memory queue in nanoseconds, while a background disk I/O thread flushes batches to disk without slowing down user transactions.
conceptual_breakdown: Asynchronous Ring Buffer: Thread-safe blocking queue decoupling caller threads from slow disk writes.
Graceful Shutdown: Flushes all pending log entries during application termination.

steps.description: Worker threads push LogEvent('Order Created') into Ring Buffer in 15ns.
Background Flush Thread wakes up on condition variable notification.
Swaps active queue with empty queue in O(1) pointer swap, minimizing lock hold time.
Writes batch to Disk File and Network Sinks without holding the incoming queue lock.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Double-Buffering Queue Swap: localBatch.swap(queue) extracts all pending log items in $O(1)$ time and releases the mutex immediately so application threads are never blocked by slow disk I/O.
2. Observer / Strategy Pattern for Sinks: ILogAppender allows dynamically attaching file sinks, console printers, and syslog network forwarders.
3. Graceful Shutdown Guarantee: The destructor signals isRunning = false, notifies the condition variable, and joins the worker thread after draining remaining queued entries.

comparison_matrix.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Logging
rows: Unflushed memory buffer may be lost if process SIGKILLs

common_mistakes.mistake: Performing disk write `file << msg` while holding the queue lock
common_mistakes.correction: Swap the queue into a local batch and write to disk outside the critical section.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'What happens if application threads generate 1,000,000 logs/sec and the disk can only write 100,000/sec?'
Answer: Discuss backpressure policies: Bounded Queue with either Drop Oldest Logs, Drop Debug Logs, or Block Application Caller Thread.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a synchronous logging class that opens a file on every log call into an asynchronous queue.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: ofstream file("app.log", ios::app); file << msg; // Opens file every time
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: AsyncLogger with background worker and persistent open file stream.

practice_problem.title: Design Log File Rolling by Size & Date
practice_problem.description: Implement a `RollingFileAppender` that automatically renames and compresses `app.log` to `app.2026-10-03.1.gz` when file size exceeds 100 MB.
practice_problem.hint: Check `std::filesystem::file_size` before write; rotate file handle when threshold reached.
